title: Your first heading
task: Make a big heading that says Hello, and a paragraph under it that says I am learning HTML.
solution:
Hello

I am learning HTML.
walkthrough:
Hello

is a level 1 heading, the top level. Headings go from h1 (most important) to h6 (least). It shows big and bold because of the browser's default styles. You can change the look with CSS.

I am learning HTML.

is a paragraph. It starts on its own line because p is a block element. The two elements sit next to each other, not inside each other. They are siblings. Common mistake: picking h1, h2 or h3 for their size. Pick the level by meaning, and set the size with CSS.

title: A link
task: Make a link with the text Google that goes to https://google.com and opens in a new tab.
solution: Google
walkthrough: closes the link. Common mistake: writing href="google.com" without https://. The browser reads it as a file next to the current page, not as the Google site.

title: A shopping list
task: Make a bulleted list with three items: Milk, Eggs, Bread.
solution:
• Milk
  • Eggs
  • Bread
walkthrough:
opens an unordered list. Each item gets a bullet.
  • Milk
    • is one list item. All three li elements are children of the ul. Each li closes before the next one opens, and the ul closes after the last li. The order in the code is the order on the page. Common mistake: putting text or a p straight inside the ul. Only li elements belong directly inside a ul; put everything else inside an li.

title: An image with alt text
task: Show the image https://picsum.photos/200 with the alt text A random photo, inside a figure with the caption Random.

title: A sign-up form
task: Make a form with a labeled email input (id email, required) and a Sign up submit button.
solution:
<form>
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" type="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
walkthrough:
<form> wraps the fields that are sent together.
<label for="email">Email</label> names the field. for matches the input's id, so clicking the label focuses the input and screen readers read the label with it.
<input id="email" type="email" required> is a void element. type="email" makes the browser check the text looks like an email address.
required is a boolean attribute: just being there means true, no value needed. The form will not send while the field is empty.
<button type="submit">Sign up</button> sends the form when clicked.
Common mistake: making for match the input's name or class instead of its id. Then the label is not linked to the field.

title: A table

solution:

opens the table. is a table row. Each row holds cells. is a header cell. It labels its column, and browsers show it bold and centered by default. is a data cell, a normal value. The second row has two td, so they line up under the two th. The browser adds a tbody around the rows for you, even though it is not written. Common mistake: giving rows different numbers of cells. The table gets a ragged edge, with a gap where a cell is missing.
NameAda

title: A page layout
task: Build a page with a header, a nav with two links, a main with an article, and a footer.
solution:
My site
Home About

Post

Text

© 2026
walkthrough:
<header>My site</header> holds the intro of the page, like the site name.
<nav> holds the main navigation links. href="/" is the root of the site; href="/about" is the about page on the same site.
<main> holds the main content of the page. A page should have only one visible main.
<article> is a piece that stands on its own, like a blog post. Here it nests an h2 and a p.
<footer> holds closing info, like the copyright line.
Common mistake: using div for all of these. It looks the same, but screen readers lose the meaning, so users cannot jump straight to the nav or the main content.

title: An FAQ without JavaScript
task: Make a question that hides its answer until clicked: the summary is What is HTML? and the answer is The structure of a web page.
solution:
<details>
  <summary>What is HTML?</summary>
  The structure of a web page.
</details>
mustInclude: The structure of a web page.
walkthrough:
<details> makes a box that opens and closes. It starts closed.
<summary>What is HTML?</summary> is the part that is always shown. Clicking it opens or closes the box.
The text after the summary is the answer. It shows only while the box is open.
The browser does the toggling, so no JavaScript is needed. Add the open attribute to start it open.
Common mistake: leaving out summary. The browser then shows its own label, usually "Details", which tells the reader nothing.

title: An icon link
task: Make a link to planner.html showing • that screen readers skip and Tab skips, then a normal link to planner.html with the text Planner.
remember: aria-hidden = hidden from assistive tech; tabindex -1 = no Tab stop.
solution: • Planner
walkthrough: • is a link to a file in the same folder as the current page. aria-hidden="true" hides the element from screen readers. A dot means nothing when read aloud. tabindex="-1" takes it out of the Tab order. A mouse can still click it. The second link, with the text Planner, is the one screen readers and keyboard users get. Nobody hears or tabs through the same link twice. Common mistake: using aria-hidden="true" without tabindex="-1". Keyboard users can still Tab onto the link, and a screen reader lands on something it was told to hide.

title: Draw a box lid
task: Draw a 24×24 SVG with one path: a diamond from 4 7.5 to 12 3 to 20 7.5 to 12 12, closed. Outline only, in the text colour.
remember: M = Move, L = Line, Z = Zip it closed.
solution:
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor">
  <path d="M4 7.5 L12 3 L20 7.5 L12 12 Z"/>
</svg>
walkthrough:
<svg opens a drawing. viewBox="0 0 24 24" sets its own grid: start at 0 0, 24 units wide, 24 tall. width and height set the size on the page.
fill="none" means no fill inside shapes. stroke="currentColor" draws the outline in the current text color. The path inside inherits both.
<path d="..."/> is the shape. d is a list of drawing commands. M4 7.5 moves the pen to x 4, y 7.5 without drawing.
L12 3 draws a straight line to 12 3, and so on. Z closes the shape with a line back to the start.
The /> closes the path in the same tag, which is allowed inside SVG.
Common mistake: forgetting that y grows downward in SVG. 12 3 is near the top; 12 12 is lower down.

title: Two tabs
task: Make a tablist with two tab buttons (Practice is selected, Examples is not), each pointing at its panel with aria-controls. Then two tabpanel sections; the Examples one is hidden.
remember: list → tab → panel. aria-controls = the id of the panel.
solution:
Practice
Examples
walkthrough:
<div role="tablist"> tells screen readers this div is a row of tabs. role changes what assistive tech says the element is, not how it looks or works.
<button role="tab"> is one tab. aria-controls="practice" points at the id of the panel this tab controls.
aria-selected="true" marks the current tab; the other has "false". You must change these yourself with JavaScript when the user switches tabs.
<section id="practice" role="tabpanel"> is the content for one tab. Its id is what aria-controls points at.
hidden is a boolean attribute. The browser does not show the element.
Common mistake: thinking the roles make the tabs work. They only describe. Clicking does nothing until a script swaps aria-selected and hidden.

title: Stop the bubble
task: Make a div with id="day" holding a button with id="dot". In a script, clicking the day shows "open" in the day; clicking the dot shows "tick" on the dot and uses event.stopPropagation() so the day does not open too. Click the dot to try it.
solution: day
remember: Events bubble up; stopPropagation pops the bubble.
walkthrough:
<div id="day"> holds a button with id="dot". The button is nested inside the div.
addEventListener("click", ...) runs a function each time the element is clicked. The day's function adds the text " open".
A click on the dot bubbles: the dot's listener runs, then the click travels up to the day and its listener runs too.
event.stopPropagation() stops that trip up, so the day's listener never runs. event.target is the element clicked, the button, and its text becomes "tick".
The script comes after the HTML, so the elements already exist when getElementById looks for them.
Common mistake: writing event.stopPropagation without (). That only names the method and does not call it, so the click still bubbles.

title: Core: one rule
task: Write a rule for .note that sets color to red and padding to 10px.
remember: WHO { WHAT: HOW; }
walkthrough:
.note is the selector. The dot means "class", so it picks every element with class="note".
The curly braces hold the declarations for that selector.
color: red; is one declaration: a property, a colon, a value, a semicolon. color sets the text color.
padding: 10px; adds 10px of space inside the element, between its content and its border. That is the padding layer of the box model.
Common mistake: forgetting the dot and writing note { ... }. That looks for a tag called note, so nothing matches.

title: Core: a rule wrapping rules
task: Make a custom property --ink: blue on :root, use it with var() on p, and wrap a rule inside @media (max-width: 600px) that sets p { font-size: 14px; }.
remember: -- makes it, var() uses it, @media wraps rules.
walkthrough:
:root picks the top element of the page, the html element. --ink: blue; makes a custom property. Its name must start with two dashes.
Custom properties inherit, so every element on the page can read --ink.
p { color: var(--ink); } reads it back. var() puts the value in its place, so the text is blue.
@media (max-width: 600px) is an at-rule. It wraps normal rules and applies them only while the viewport is 600px wide or less.
Inside it, p { font-size: 14px; } is an ordinary rule.
Common mistake: writing var(ink) or var(-ink). The name in var() must match exactly, both dashes included, or the declaration does not work.

title: Color a heading
task: Make every h1 red.
solution: h1 { color: red; }
walkthrough:
h1 is a type selector. With no dot or hash, it matches a tag name, so it picks every h1 on the page.
{ opens the declaration block and } closes it.
color: red; sets the text color. color is the property, red is a named color value.
The last semicolon in a block is optional, but writing it keeps you safe when you add another line.
Common mistake: writing colour: red. CSS uses American spelling. The browser drops a property it does not know, and the text keeps its default color.

title: Rounded box
task: Give .box a 1px solid black border, 10px of padding and rounded corners of 8px.
walkthrough:
.box picks every element with class="box".
border: 1px solid black; is a shorthand. It sets the width, the style and the color of all four borders in one line.
padding: 10px; puts 10px of space inside the border, around the content. In the box model, padding sits between content and border.
border-radius: 8px; rounds each corner with an 8px radius. The background and the border follow the curve.
Common mistake: leaving out the style, as in border: 1px black. The style then defaults to none, so no border shows.

title: Side by side
task: Make .row put its children side by side with flexbox and a 12px gap.
solution: .row { display: flex; gap: 12px; }
walkthrough:
.row { display: flex; } makes .row a flex container. Its direct children become flex items and line up in a row by default.
Only direct children are affected. Elements nested deeper keep their normal layout.
gap: 12px; puts 12px of space between items, but not before the first or after the last.
Common mistake: putting display: flex on the children instead of the parent. Flex is set on the container; the items line up because their parent is flex.

title: Hover button
task: Make .button turn black with white text when you point at it.
solution: .button:hover { background: black; color: white; }
walkthrough:
.button:hover is a selector with a pseudo-class. :hover matches while the mouse pointer is over the element.
The rule applies only during hover. When the pointer leaves, the button goes back to its normal styles.
background: black; is a shorthand; here it sets the background color.
color: white; sets the text color, so the text stays readable on black.
Common mistake: adding a space, as in .button :hover. That means "any hovered element inside .button", not the button itself.

title: A 3-column grid
task: Make .grid a grid with 3 equal columns.
solution: .grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; }
walkthrough:
display: grid; makes .grid a grid container. Its direct children become grid items.
grid-template-columns sets the columns. Each value in the list is one column.
1fr means one fraction of the free space. Three 1fr values split the width into three equal columns.
Items fill the cells left to right, then start a new row by themselves.
Common mistake: writing grid-template-columns: 3; to mean three columns. That value is invalid, so the browser ignores it. Use 1fr 1fr 1fr or repeat(3, 1fr).

title: Center anything
task: Center the content of .parent both ways using grid.
solution: .parent { display: grid; place-items: center; }
walkthrough:
display: grid; makes .parent a grid container. With no columns set, there is one column, and each child gets its own row.
place-items: center; is a shorthand for align-items and justify-items. It centers each item in its grid area, both up and down and side to side.
To see the up-and-down centering, the parent must be taller than its content, for example by giving it a height.
Common mistake: putting place-items: center on the child. It belongs on the grid container; the child moves because its parent says so.

title: Theme variables
task: Make a --main color variable on :root set to tomato, and use it as the background of .button.
solution:
:root { --main: tomato; }
.button { background: var(--main); }
walkthrough:
:root picks the html element, the top of the page. A variable set there reaches everything, because custom properties inherit.
--main: tomato; defines a custom property. tomato is a real CSS named color.
.button { background: var(--main); } reads the variable. var() puts tomato in its place.
Change --main in one place and every rule that uses it changes too. That is why themes use variables.
Common mistake: defining the variable inside .button and using it in another selector. A custom property only reaches its element and that element's descendants, so elsewhere var(--main) finds nothing.

title: Mobile first
task: Make .grid one column by default, and 3 columns on screens 900px or wider.
walkthrough:
The first rule is the default for every screen: .grid is a grid with one column, and 1fr takes all the width.
@media (min-width: 900px) is an at-rule. The rules inside apply only when the viewport is 900px wide or more.
Inside it, the .grid rule changes only grid-template-columns. display: grid still comes from the first rule.
repeat(3, 1fr) is short for 1fr 1fr 1fr: three equal columns.
Both rules use the same selector, so when the media query matches, the later one in the file wins. That is the cascade.
Common mistake: putting the @media block before the default rule. With equal specificity the default then comes later and wins, so the 3 columns never show.

title: Phone layout
task: The .row has 3 boxes side by side. On screens 520px wide or less, make it one column (display: grid with grid-template-columns: 1fr).
remember: max-width = "up to this wide": the rules only count on small screens.
walkthrough:
@media (max-width: 520px) wraps rules that apply only when the viewport is 520px wide or less.
Inside it, .row { ... } is an ordinary rule nested in the at-rule.
display: grid; switches .row to a grid. It beats the earlier display value because it comes later in the file with the same selector.
grid-template-columns: 1fr; makes one column that takes the full width, so the boxes stack.
Above 520px the query does not match, and the side-by-side layout stays.
Common mistake: leaving out the parentheses, as in @media max-width: 520px. The query is invalid, so the rules inside never apply.

title: Line numbers
task: Number the three boxes in .row with a CSS counter: reset it on .row, add one on each .row div, and show it before each with ::before.
remember: Like a tally clicker: reset, increment, show.
walkthrough:
.row { counter-reset: n; } creates a counter named n on .row and sets it to 0.
.row div { counter-increment: n; } adds 1 to n for each div inside .row. The space in the selector means "inside".
.row div::before makes a pseudo-element: an extra box placed as the first child of each div.
content: counter(n) ". "; fills that box with the counter's current value, then the text ". ". You see 1. 2. 3.
Without content, ::before is not drawn at all.
Common mistake: putting counter-reset on each div. Every div then starts again at 0 and adds 1, so every box shows 1.

title: Bounce
task: Make an animation called bounce: at 0% and 100% no move, at 30% translateY(-5px) and scale(1.12). Play it on the h1 when you point at it, for 0.6s.
remember: 0% = start, 100% = end, the rest are stops on the way.
walkthrough:
@keyframes bounce is an at-rule that names an animation. Inside it are steps, not selectors.
0%, 30% and 100% are keyframes: points in time along the animation. Each one says what transform is at that moment.
translateY(-5px) moves up 5px, because negative y is up. scale(1.12) makes it 12% bigger. Both go in one transform, separated by a space.
The browser fills in the frames between the steps.
h1:hover { animation: bounce 0.6s ease; } plays it while the pointer is over the h1. animation is a shorthand: name, duration, timing function.
Common mistake: leaving out the duration. It defaults to 0s, so the animation finishes instantly and you see nothing.

title: A bubble from an attribute
task: Show the button's class name in a bubble under it with ::after and attr(class). Put the button in position: relative and the bubble in position: absolute at top: calc(100% + 10px). The bubble must not block clicks.
remember: attr() reads the attribute; top: 100% = just below the parent; pointer-events: none = a ghost.
walkthrough:
.button { position: relative; } makes the button the reference box for absolutely positioned things inside it. On its own it does not move the button.
.button::after adds a pseudo-element as the last child of the button. content: attr(class); fills it with the text of the button's class attribute.
position: absolute; takes the bubble out of normal flow and places it against the nearest positioned ancestor, here the button.
top: calc(100% + 10px); puts the bubble's top edge 10px below the bottom of the button. left: 0; lines it up with the button's left edge.
pointer-events: none; lets clicks pass through the bubble to whatever is under it.
Common mistake: forgetting position: relative on the button. The bubble then positions itself against an outer element, often the whole page, and lands far away.

title: The more specific one wins
task: Give .plan a margin-left of auto. Then write a second rule, .footer-nav .plan, that sets margin-left to 0, so plans in the footer sit on the left.
solution:
.plan { margin-left: auto; }
.footer-nav .plan { margin-left: 0; }
remember: Count the classes: more wins.
walkthrough:
.plan { margin-left: auto; } sets the left margin to auto. In a flex row, an auto margin takes up the spare space, which pushes the plan to the right.
.footer-nav .plan has two class selectors with a space between: a .plan that is inside a .footer-nav.
Both rules set margin-left on the same element. The cascade picks the more specific selector, and two classes beat one.
So in the footer, margin-left: 0 wins and the plan sits on the left. Everywhere else the first rule still applies.
Specificity counts before order: even if you swapped the two rules, the footer one would still win.
Common mistake: writing .footer-nav.plan with no space. That means one element with both classes, not a .plan inside a .footer-nav.

title: Core: values and functions
task: Make a function add(a, b) that returns a + b. Store add(2, 3) in a const called total and print it.
remember: Name it, ( ) to call it, return to answer.
walkthrough:
function add(a, b) makes a function named add with two inputs, a and b.
return a + b sends the sum back to whoever called it.
add(2, 3) calls it: a is 2, b is 3, so it returns 5.
const total keeps that 5 under a name, and console.log(total) prints 5.
Common mistake: forgetting return. The function then gives back undefined, and undefined is printed.

title: Core: an object with a method
task: Make an object pet with name "Mo" and a method speak() that returns name + " says hi". Print pet.speak().
remember: A method is a function inside an object.
walkthrough:
const pet = { ... } makes an object: a bundle of named values.
name: "Mo" is a plain value. speak() { ... } is a function stored inside the object, which is called a method.
pet.speak() uses the dot to reach the method, and the ( ) call it.
Inside the method, this is the object before the dot, so this.name is "Mo" and it returns "Mo says hi".
console.log prints that string: Mo says hi.
Common mistake: writing speak as an arrow function, speak: () => this.name + " says hi". Arrow functions do not get their own this, so this.name is undefined and it prints "undefined says hi".

title: Core: a function as an argument
task: Make a function run(fn) that calls fn twice. Call run with an arrow function that prints tick. (This is how addEventListener works.)
remember: Pass the function, don't call it: fn, not fn().
walkthrough:
function run(fn) takes one input, fn, and expects it to be a function.
Inside, fn(); fn(); calls that function twice.
run(() => console.log("tick")) passes an arrow function as the argument. It is not called yet, just handed over.
run calls it two times, so tick is printed on two lines.
Common mistake: writing run(console.log("tick")). That calls console.log right away, prints tick once, and passes its result, undefined, to run. Then fn() fails with TypeError: fn is not a function.

title: Say hello
task: Print Hello, world! with console.log.
solution: console.log("Hello, world!");
walkthrough:
console is an object Node gives you, and log is a method on it. The dot reaches the method.
The ( ) call it, and what goes inside is the value to print.
"Hello, world!" is a string value. The quotes mark where the text starts and ends; they are not printed.
So the line prints Hello, world!
Common mistake: leaving out the quotes. JavaScript then tries to read Hello as code, not text, and the line fails with an error.

title: Variables
task: Make a const name set to "Ada" and print Hi Ada using a template string.
solution:
const name = "Ada";
console.log(`Hi ${name}`);
walkthrough:
const name = "Ada" stores the string "Ada" under the name name. const means it cannot be reassigned later.
`Hi ${name}` is a template literal: a string written with backticks.
${name} inside it is replaced by the value of name, so the string becomes "Hi Ada".
console.log prints Hi Ada.
Common mistake: using normal quotes, "Hi ${name}". Only backticks fill in ${ }, so it prints Hi ${name} as plain text.

title: Count to five
task: Use a for loop to print the numbers 1 to 5, one per line.
walkthrough:
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) has three parts: start, condition, step.
let i = 1 makes a counter that starts at 1. let is used because the value changes.
Before each round, i <= 5 is checked. If it is true, the body runs; if false, the loop stops.
The body console.log(i) prints the current number, then i++ adds 1.
So it prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, each on its own line.
Common mistake: writing i < 5. The loop stops before 5, so only 1 to 4 are printed.

title: Even numbers
task: From [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] print only the even numbers as an array, using filter.
solution:
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
console.log(nums.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0));
walkthrough:
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] makes an array, an ordered list of values.
nums.filter(...) is a method call that takes a function and keeps only the items where that function returns true.
(n) => n % 2 === 0 gets each number as n. % gives the remainder after dividing by 2, and === 0 checks it is zero, so it is true for even numbers.
filter returns a new array [2, 4, 6] and leaves nums unchanged. console.log prints it as [ 2, 4, 6 ].
Common mistake: adding braces, (n) => { n % 2 === 0 }. With braces the arrow needs return, so every call gives undefined and the result is [].

title: Total price
task: The cart is [{ price: 3 }, { price: 7 }, { price: 10 }]. Print the total using reduce.
solution:
const cart = [{ price: 3 }, { price: 7 }, { price: 10 }];
console.log(cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0));
walkthrough:
cart is an array of objects, each with a price.
cart.reduce(fn, 0) walks the array and carries one running value. The 0 is where that value starts.
For each item, (sum, item) => sum + item.price returns the new running total: 0 + 3 = 3, 3 + 7 = 10, 10 + 10 = 20.
reduce returns the last total, 20, and console.log prints 20.
Common mistake: leaving out the 0. Then the first object itself becomes sum, and adding a number to an object makes a string, so it prints [object Object]710.

title: FizzBuzz
task: Print 1 to 15. For multiples of 3 print Fizz, of 5 print Buzz, of both print FizzBuzz.
expected:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
walkthrough:
The for loop runs i from 1 to 15.
i % 15 === 0 checks if i divides evenly by 15. If so it prints FizzBuzz and skips the other branches.
else if checks the next condition only when the one before was false: divisible by 3 prints Fizz, by 5 prints Buzz.
The final else prints the number itself when none matched.
So 3 prints Fizz, 5 prints Buzz, 15 prints FizzBuzz, and the rest print as numbers.
Common mistake: checking % 3 first. Then 15 matches that branch, prints Fizz, and FizzBuzz never shows.

title: Count words
task: Count each word in "the cat and the hat" and print the object, like { the: 2, cat: 1, ... }.
walkthrough:
const counts = {} makes an empty object. It will map each word to how many times it appears.
"the cat and the hat".split(" ") cuts the string at each space and returns an array of 5 words.
for (const word of ...) gives you one word at a time.
counts[word] uses square brackets because the key is in a variable. (counts[word] || 0) is 0 the first time, since a missing key is undefined; then 1 is added and stored back.
After the loop, console.log(counts) prints { the: 2, cat: 1, and: 1, hat: 1 }.
Common mistake: writing counts.word. The dot uses the literal key "word", so everything is counted under one key named word.

title: A class
task: Make a class BankAccount with deposit(amount) and a balance. Deposit 50 then 25, then print the balance.
walkthrough:
class BankAccount { ... } is a blueprint for making objects.
constructor() runs once when an object is made. this.balance = 0 gives the new object a balance of 0.
deposit(amount) is a method. this.balance += amount adds the amount to that object's balance.
new BankAccount() makes the object. account.deposit(50) then account.deposit(25) bring balance to 75.
console.log(account.balance) reads the property with the dot and prints 75.
Common mistake: forgetting new, BankAccount(). Classes cannot be called that way, and you get TypeError: Class constructor BankAccount cannot be invoked without 'new'.

title: Count the letters
task: Print how many characters "日本語😀" has, counting the emoji as one.
remember: Spread it out, then count: [...text].length.
solution:
const text = "日本語😀";
console.log([...text].length);
walkthrough:
const text = "日本語😀" is a string of four characters as you see them.
JavaScript stores strings as UTF-16 code units. The emoji needs two of them, so text.length is 5.
[...text] spreads the string into an array. Spreading goes by code point, so the emoji stays as one item.
The array has 4 items, so [...text].length is 4 and that is printed.
Common mistake: using text.length to count characters. It prints 5 here, because it counts code units, not characters.

title: Keys that do things
task: Make an object KEYS where d gives "day" and w gives "week" (each as a function). Print what KEYS["w"] gives when you call it.
remember: Look it up, then call it: KEYS[key]().
walkthrough:
const KEYS = { ... } is an object where each value is a function.
d: () => "day" is an arrow function that returns "day". w returns "week".
KEYS["w"] looks up the key "w" with square brackets and gets the function, not its result.
The () after it calls that function, which returns "week". console.log prints week.
Common mistake: leaving off the (). KEYS["w"] alone is the function itself, so Node prints [Function: w] instead of week.

title: A date to save by
task: From new Date(2026, 0, 5), print 2026-01-05 (with the zeros).
remember: getMonth() + 1 because January is 0. padStart(2, "0") adds the zero.
walkthrough:
new Date(2026, 0, 5) makes a date. The month is counted from 0, so 0 means January: this is 5 January 2026.
d.getFullYear() gives 2026. d.getMonth() gives 0, so + 1 turns it into the real month number, 1.
String(...) turns the number into text, and .padStart(2, "0") adds a 0 in front until it is 2 characters long: "01". The day becomes "05" the same way.
The + signs join the pieces into one string, and console.log(key) prints 2026-01-05.
Common mistake: forgetting the + 1 on getMonth(). January comes out as 00, so it prints 2026-00-05.

title: Heading or not
task: Write kind(line): for a line starting with 1 to 6 # and a space, give "h" + the number of # + ": " + the rest; otherwise "text: " + the line. Print kind("## Shopping") and kind("hello").
remember: match gives null or [whole, group 1, group 2]. ( ) = capture.
walkthrough:
function kind(line) takes one line of text and returns a label for it.
line.match(/^(#{1,6}) (.*)/) tests a regular expression: ^ is the start, #{1,6} is 1 to 6 # signs, then a space, then (.*) is the rest. The ( ) parts are captured.
If it matches, m is an array: m[1] is the # signs and m[2] is the rest. If not, m is null.
For "## Shopping", m[1] is "##" with length 2, so it returns "h2: Shopping".
For "hello", m is null, the if is skipped, and it returns "text: hello". The two console.log lines print those two results.
Common mistake: using m[0] for the text. m[0] is the whole match, "## Shopping", not just the part after the space.

title: Mark it done
task: Write markDone(line): "• x" becomes "× x", "× x" becomes "• x", anything else stays the same. Print markDone("• buy milk"), markDone("× buy milk") and markDone("– a note").
remember: line[0] is the bullet, line.slice(2) is the text after "• ".
expected:
× buy milk
• buy milk
– a note
walkthrough:
function markDone(line) takes a line and returns it with its mark flipped.
line.slice(2) drops the first 2 characters, the mark and the space, so text is "buy milk".
line[0] reads the first character. If it is •, it returns "× " + text. If it is ×, it returns "• " + text.
return ends the function right there, so only one branch ever runs. Any other line, like the – note, falls through to return line unchanged.
The three calls print × buy milk, • buy milk, and – a note.
Common mistake: using line.slice(1). That keeps the space after the mark, so the result has two spaces, like ×  buy milk.

title: Time stamp
task: Like the planner's /t: write timeStamp(text, date). If text ends with "/t " (at the start or after a space), swap it for the time from date as HH:MM and a space; otherwise give text back. Print timeStamp("meeting /t ", new Date(2026, 10, 27, 14, 5)), timeStamp("/t ", new Date(2026, 10, 27, 9, 30)) and timeStamp("a/t ", new Date()).
remember: toTimeString().slice(0, 5) = HH:MM. An object of functions: SLASH[word](date).
walkthrough:
SLASH is an object whose t key holds a function. date.toTimeString() gives text like "14:05:00 GMT...", and .slice(0, 5) keeps "14:05".
In timeStamp, text.match(...) looks for a / at the start or after a space, then a word, then one space at the very end. (\w+) captures the word, so word[1] is "t".
If there is no match, or SLASH has no function for that word, it returns the text unchanged. The ! means "not".
start = text.length - word[1].length - 2 finds where the / is: the 2 counts the / and the final space.
It keeps the text before the /, adds SLASH["t"](date), which calls the function, and adds a space back. So it prints "meeting 14:05 " and "09:30 ".
Common mistake: expecting "a/t " to change. The / must be at the start or after a space, so the match fails and it prints a/t unchanged, which is on purpose here.

title: Split a line
task: lines is ["a", "bc", "d"]. Like pressing Enter in the middle of "bc": replace it with "b" and "c" using splice, then print the lines joined with commas.
remember: splice(where, how many to remove, …what to add).
walkthrough:
const lines = ["a", "bc", "d"] makes an array. const stops you reassigning lines, but the array itself can still change.
lines.splice(1, 1, "b", "c") goes to index 1, removes 1 item ("bc"), and puts "b" and "c" in its place.
splice changes the array itself, so lines is now ["a", "b", "c", "d"].
lines.join(",") glues the items into one string with commas between them, and console.log prints a,b,c,d.
Common mistake: doing const result = lines.splice(...) and printing result. splice returns the removed items, so you get [ 'bc' ], not the new array.

title: Monday of the week
task: Write monday(date) that gives the Monday of that week (weeks start on Monday). Print the day of the month for new Date(2026, 10, 27) (a Friday) and new Date(2026, 10, 29) (a Sunday).
remember: getDay: Sunday is 0. (getDay() + 6) % 7 = days since Monday.
walkthrough:
function monday(date) returns the Monday of the same week.
new Date(date) makes a copy, so the date passed in is not changed.
copy.getDay() gives 0 for Sunday up to 6 for Saturday. (getDay() + 6) % 7 turns that into days since Monday: Monday 0, Sunday 6.
copy.setDate(copy.getDate() - that) moves the copy back that many days.
27 November 2026 is a Friday, 4 days after Monday, so 27 - 4 = 23. The 29th is a Sunday, 6 days after Monday, so 29 - 6 = 23. Both lines print 23.
Common mistake: using copy.getDay() - 1. For a Sunday that is -1, so it moves forward one day to the next Monday instead of back.

title: Next Friday
task: Write nextDay(today, word) that finds the day name starting with word (like "fri") and returns how many days until the next one (not today: use 7 then). Today is a Friday (day 5). Print nextDay(5, "fri"), nextDay(5, "mon") and nextDay(5, "sat").
remember: % 7 wraps the week around; || 7 turns "0 days" into "next week".
walkthrough:
DAYS is an array of day names; each index is the day number, with sunday at 0.
DAYS.findIndex(...) returns the index of the first name where the function is true. name.startsWith(word) lets "fri" match "friday", giving 5.
(n - today + 7) % 7 counts days forward. The + 7 keeps it from going negative before the %.
|| 7 replaces a 0 with 7, because 0 is falsy. So the same day means next week, not today.
With today = 5 (Friday): fri gives 0 then 7, mon gives 3, sat gives 1. It prints 7, 3, 1.
Common mistake: leaving out || 7. Then asking for Friday on a Friday returns 0, meaning today.

title: Move a task
task: Today is Friday 27 November 2026. Write moveTo(line): if the line ends with @ and a day name (like @fri or @mon), print the line without the @word, then the date of the next one as "Fri 4 Dec". Try "• call mum @fri" and "• pay rent @mon".
remember: Find the @word with a regex, the day with findIndex, the gap with % 7 || 7.
expected:
• call mum
Fri 4 Dec
• pay rent
Mon 30 Nov
walkthrough:
today is a fixed date, 27 November 2026, a Friday. DAYS and MONTHS are arrays used to turn numbers into names.
line.match(...) finds @word at the end of the line, so m[1] is "fri". findIndex gives its day number n, here 5.
new Date(today) copies today. setDate(today.getDate() + ...) moves the copy forward by the days until that weekday, using 7 if it is the same day. setDate handles rolling into December.
line.replace(/\s*@\w+\s*$/, "") removes the @word and the spaces around it, so it prints • call mum.
The next line builds a name: DAYS[...][0].toUpperCase() makes the first letter capital, .slice(1) adds the rest, then the day number and month name. It prints Fri 4 Dec, then • pay rent and Mon 30 Nov.
Common mistake: forgetting the copy and calling setDate on today itself. today then changes, and the second call counts from the wrong day.

title: Count down (recursion)
task: Write countDown(n) that prints n, then calls itself with n - 1, and prints go when n is 0. Call countDown(3).
remember: A stop case first, then a smaller step.
walkthrough:
function countDown(n) is recursive: it calls itself.
if (n === 0) is the base case. It prints go, and return stops this call.
Otherwise it prints n, then calls countDown(n - 1) with a smaller number.
countDown(3) prints 3, then countDown(2) prints 2, then 1, then countDown(0) prints go.
Common mistake: forgetting the return in the base case. After go it keeps going, prints 0, calls countDown(-1), never reaches 0 again, and crashes with RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

title: Add a project
task: Here is a list of projects: home (index.html) and planner (planner.html). Add a third object for japanese (japanese.html). Then loop over the list with for...of and print each one as "name: href".
remember: Data in a list, code in a loop. Add a line, not code.
expected:
home: index.html
planner: planner.html
japanese: japanese.html
walkthrough:
PROJECTS is an array of objects. Each object has two properties, name and href.
for (const project of PROJECTS) gives you each object in order, one per round.
project.name and project.href read the properties with the dot.
The + signs join them with ": " in between, so it prints home: index.html, then the planner and japanese lines.
Common mistake: using for...in instead of for...of. for...in gives the indexes "0", "1", "2", which have no name, so it prints undefined: undefined.

title: Tasks on top
task: Sort ["notes", "• call mum", "idea", "• buy milk", "end"] so the lines starting with "• " come first, and the other lines keep their order. Use sort with a comparator that subtracts two booleans. Print each line.
remember: true - false = 1, so b - a puts the trues first. Sort keeps ties in order.
expected:
• call mum
• buy milk
notes
idea
end
walkthrough:
lines is an array of strings. isTask is an arrow function that returns true when a line starts with "• ".
[...lines] copies the array first, because sort changes the array it is called on.
.sort((a, b) => isTask(b) - isTask(a)) compares two lines at a time. Subtracting booleans turns them into numbers, 1 for true and 0 for false.
If b is a task and a is not, the result is 1, which puts b first. When both are the same, it is 0, and sort keeps their original order.
So the two tasks come first, then notes, idea, end, and the for...of loop prints each line.
Common mistake: sorting lines directly without the copy. It works, but the original lines array is changed too, which surprises any code that still uses it.

title: Core: a module
task: require the path module and print path.join("data", "css.json").
solution:
const path = require("path");
console.log(path.join("data", "css.json"));
remember: require = give me that toolbox.
walkthrough:
require("path") loads Node's built-in path module and returns an object full of functions.
const path keeps that object under a name.
path.join is a method on that object. It joins its string arguments with the right separator for the system.
On macOS or Linux the separator is /, so it prints data/css.json. On Windows it would use a backslash.
Common mistake: using path without the require line. In a script file it is not defined, so you get ReferenceError: path is not defined.

title: Core: a callback later
task: Print first, then use setTimeout with 0 ms to print second, then print third. Watch the order.
remember: Callbacks run after the rest of your code.
walkthrough:
console.log("first") runs right away and prints first.
setTimeout(fn, 0) does not run fn now. It schedules it to run later, after at least 0 ms.
Node keeps going, and console.log("third") prints third.
Only after the rest of the code has finished does Node run the timer callback, which prints second.
Common mistake: thinking a 0 delay means "right now". The callback still waits until the current code is done, so second comes last.

title: Built-in modules
task: Load the built-in os module with require, and print what type os.homedir() gives back (use typeof).
solution:
const os = require("os");
console.log(typeof os.homedir());
walkthrough:
require("os") loads the built-in os module, an object with information about the computer.
os.homedir() calls a method that returns the path of your home folder as a string.
typeof is an operator that gives the type of a value as text.
So typeof os.homedir() is "string" and console.log prints string.
Common mistake: leaving off the (), typeof os.homedir. That asks about the method itself, not its result, so it prints function.

title: Join paths
task: Use path.join to join "users", "ada" and "notes.txt" and print it.
solution:
const path = require("path");
console.log(path.join("users", "ada", "notes.txt"));
walkthrough:
require("path") loads the built-in path module, and const path stores it.
path.join("users", "ada", "notes.txt") takes three strings and joins them into one path.
It puts the system's separator between them, / on macOS and Linux, and cleans up doubled slashes.
console.log prints users/ada/notes.txt.
Common mistake: writing require("Path") with a capital P. Module names must match exactly, so Node throws Cannot find module 'Path'.

title: Write and read a file
task: Write Hello file into hello.txt, then read it back and print it.
walkthrough:
require("fs") loads the built-in file system module.
fs.writeFileSync("hello.txt", "Hello file") creates the file, or replaces it, with that text. Sync means Node waits until it is done before the next line.
fs.readFileSync("hello.txt", "utf8") reads the file back. The "utf8" tells it to return a string.
console.log prints that string: Hello file.
Common mistake: leaving out "utf8". readFileSync then returns a Buffer, raw bytes, and it prints something like <Buffer 48 65 6c 6c 6f ...>.

title: JSON file
task: Save { "score": 10 } to score.json, read it back, add 5 and print the new score.
walkthrough:
JSON.stringify({ score: 10 }) turns the object into the text {"score":10}, because files can only hold text or bytes.
fs.writeFileSync saves that text to score.json.
fs.readFileSync("score.json", "utf8") reads it back as a string, and JSON.parse turns the string back into an object.
data.score is the number 10, so data.score + 5 is 15, and 15 is printed.
Common mistake: skipping JSON.parse. data is then a string, data.score is undefined, and undefined + 5 prints NaN.

title: Wait with await
task: Write an async function that waits 200 ms with timers/promises, then prints done.
walkthrough:
require("timers/promises") returns an object. { setTimeout: wait } takes its setTimeout property and names it wait.
This setTimeout returns a promise that settles after the given milliseconds.
async function main() is a function that may use await inside it.
await wait(200) pauses main for 200 ms without blocking Node, then console.log prints done.
main() starts it.
Common mistake: leaving out await. Then main does not pause, and done is printed right away instead of after 200 ms.

title: Events
task: Make an EventEmitter. Listen for "order" and print Order for <item>. Emit it with "coffee".
walkthrough:
require("events") returns the EventEmitter class, and new EventEmitter() makes an object that can send and receive named events.
shop.on("order", fn) is a method call with a function as an argument. It registers fn to run whenever "order" happens.
shop.emit("order", "coffee") fires the event. Every listener for "order" is called right then, with "coffee" as its argument.
So item is "coffee" and it prints Order for coffee.
Common mistake: calling emit before on. No listener exists yet, so nothing is printed.

title: List files by type
task: Create a.txt, b.txt and c.js, then print only the .txt file names, sorted, one per line.
walkthrough:
The for...of loop calls fs.writeFileSync for each name, making three empty files: a.txt, b.txt, c.js.
fs.readdirSync(".") returns an array of file names in the current folder.
.filter(...) keeps names where path.extname(f) is ".txt". extname returns the ending from the last dot, including the dot.
.sort() puts them in order, and .forEach calls console.log for each one. The methods chain, each working on the array the last one returned.
It prints a.txt and b.txt.
Common mistake: comparing to "txt" without the dot. extname returns ".txt", so nothing matches and nothing is printed.

title: Missing file
task: Try to read missing.txt with fs/promises. Catch the error and print its code.
walkthrough:
require("fs/promises") loads the promise version of fs. Its readFile returns a promise instead of the data directly.
async function main() lets you use await, which waits for the promise.
The file does not exist, so the promise is rejected. Because of await, that rejection is thrown inside try.
catch (err) catches it. err.code is a short error name, and ENOENT means no such file or directory. That is what is printed.
Common mistake: leaving out await. try then finishes before the read fails, catch never runs, and Node crashes with an unhandled rejection error.

title: Core: a block with :
task: Loop over [1, 2, 3] and print each number times 10.
solution:
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    print(n * 10)
remember: Colon opens, indent holds.
walkthrough:
for n in [1, 2, 3]: takes each value in the list, one at a time, and puts it in the name n.
The colon ends the header. The indented line under it is the block that runs once per value.
print(n * 10) multiplies the current n by 10 and prints it, so you get 10, then 20, then 30.
print puts each result on its own line, because it adds a newline at the end by default.
Common mistake: leaving off the colon after the for line. Python stops with a SyntaxError before running anything.

title: Core: def and a method
task: Write def shout(word) that returns word.upper() + "!". Print shout("hi").
remember: def + : + indent; dot asks the value.
walkthrough:
def shout(word): makes a function named shout with one input, word. The colon starts its block.
The indented line is the body: word.upper() asks the string for an upper-case copy, then + "!" adds an exclamation mark.
return sends that new string back to whoever called the function.
print(shout("hi")) calls it with "hi" and prints HI!.
Common mistake: not indenting the body. Python then raises an IndentationError, because the indent is what puts the line inside the function.

title: Say hello
task: Print Hello, world!
solution: print("Hello, world!")
walkthrough:
print is a built-in function. The parentheses call it, and what is inside them is its input.
"Hello, world!" is a string value. The quotes mark where the text starts and ends; they are not printed.
print writes the text and then a newline, so the output is Hello, world!
Common mistake: writing print "Hello, world!" without parentheses, as in old Python 2 code. Python 3 gives a SyntaxError.

title: f-strings
task: Make name = "Ada" and age = 36, then print Ada is 36 using an f-string.
solution:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
print(f"{name} is {age}")
walkthrough:
name = "Ada" puts a string value in the name name. age = 36 puts a number in age.
The f before the quotes makes it an f-string: anything inside { } is worked out and its value is dropped into the text.
{name} becomes Ada and {age} becomes 36, so the string is Ada is 36.
print shows that finished string.
Common mistake: forgetting the f. Then the braces are just text and Python prints {name} is {age} literally.

title: Count to five
task: Use a for loop and range to print 1 to 5.
solution:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)
walkthrough:
range(1, 6) gives the numbers from 1 up to, but not including, 6. So 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
for i in ...: puts each of those numbers in i, one at a time. The colon starts the block.
The indented print(i) runs once per number and prints it on its own line.
Common mistake: writing range(1, 5) or range(5). The stop number is left out, so you get 1 to 4, or 0 to 4.

title: Squares
task: Use a list comprehension to make the squares of 1 to 5 and print the list.
solution: print([n * n for n in range(1, 6)])
walkthrough:
The square brackets with a for inside are a list comprehension: a short way to build a new list.
for n in range(1, 6) walks through 1 to 5. For each n, the part before the for, n * n, is the value that goes into the list.
So the list becomes [1, 4, 9, 16, 25].
print shows the whole list, with its brackets and commas.
Common mistake: writing n ^ 2 to mean a square. In Python ^ is bitwise XOR, not power; use n * n or n ** 2.

title: Grades
task: Write a function grade(score) that returns A for 90+, B for 70+, otherwise C. Print grade(95), grade(75), grade(10).
walkthrough:
def grade(score): makes a function with one input. Everything indented under it is its body.
if score >= 90: is checked first. If it is true, return "A" sends back "A" and the function stops right there.
elif means "otherwise, if". It is only checked when the first test failed. 75 fails the first test and passes this one, so it gets "B".
If no test passed, the code falls through to return "C". That is what 10 gets.
print(grade(95), grade(75), grade(10)) prints the three results with a space between each: A B C.
Common mistake: writing score > 90 instead of score >= 90. Then a score of exactly 90 gets a B.

title: FizzBuzz
task: Print 1 to 15. For multiples of 3 print Fizz, of 5 print Buzz, of both print FizzBuzz.
expected:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
walkthrough:
for i in range(1, 16): runs the block for 1 to 15.
i % 15 is the remainder after dividing by 15. == 0 asks whether it divides evenly. A number divisible by 15 is divisible by both 3 and 5.
if, elif, elif, else is one chain. Python checks the tests top to bottom and runs only the first one that is true.
else catches numbers that matched none of the tests, and print(i) prints the number itself.
Common mistake: checking i % 3 before i % 15. Then 15 matches the Fizz test first, and FizzBuzz is never printed.

title: Word count
task: Count the words in "the cat and the hat" with a dictionary, then print each word and count, one per line, like the 2.
walkthrough:
counts = {} makes an empty dictionary: a box of key to value pairs.
"the cat and the hat".split() asks the string to cut itself at spaces, giving the list ['the', 'cat', 'and', 'the', 'hat'].
counts.get(word, 0) returns the count so far, or 0 if the word is not there yet. + 1 adds one, and counts[word] = stores it back.
counts.items() gives each key and value as a pair, and for word, n in unpacks the pair into two names.
Dictionaries keep the order keys were first added, so the output starts with the 2.
Common mistake: writing counts[word] += 1 without get. The first time a word appears it is not in the dictionary yet, so Python raises a KeyError.

title: A class
task: Make a class BankAccount with a deposit method. Deposit 50 then 25, then print the balance.
walkthrough:
class BankAccount: makes a new type of object. The indented defs inside are its methods.
__init__ runs automatically when you write BankAccount(). self is the new object, and self.balance = 0 gives it a balance of 0.
deposit(self, amount) adds amount to that object's balance with +=.
account.deposit(50) is the same as calling deposit with self set to account, so balance goes 0, 50, then 75 after the second call.
print(account.balance) reads the value and prints 75.
Common mistake: writing def deposit(amount): without self. Python still passes the object in first, so you get a TypeError about too many arguments.

title: Core: types and a function
task: Write int square(int n) that returns n * n, and print square(6) from main.
remember: Type first, then name.
walkthrough:
#include <stdio.h> brings in the declaration of printf.
int square(int n) says: a function named square that takes an int and gives back an int. Types come before names in C.
Its block in { } has one statement, return n * n; and every statement ends with ;.
main is where the program starts. square(6) runs first and gives 36, then printf puts it where %d is, followed by \n, a newline.
return 0; tells the system the program finished fine.
Common mistake: forgetting the ; after return n * n. The compiler stops with an error pointing at the next line.

title: Core: a pointer
task: Make int n = 1, a pointer p to it, set *p = 5, and print n.
remember: & = where is it, * = go there.
walkthrough:
int n = 1; makes an int variable n holding 1.
int *p = &n; makes p, a pointer to an int. &n is the address of n, so p now points at n.
*p = 5; follows the pointer and writes 5 into the thing it points at, which is n itself.
printf("%d\n", n) prints n, which is now 5, even though the code never wrote n = 5.
Common mistake: writing p = 5; without the star. That tries to change where p points instead of changing n; the compiler complains, and n would stay 1.

title: Say hello
task: Print Hello, world! with printf.
walkthrough:
#include <stdio.h> brings in printf from the standard input/output library.
int main(void) is the function where every C program starts. void means it takes no inputs, and int is the type it returns.
printf("Hello, world!\n"); prints the text. \n is a newline character. The ; ends the statement.
return 0; ends main and reports success.
Common mistake: leaving out the \n. The text still prints, but no line break follows, so the terminal prompt can end up on the same line.

title: Variables
task: Make int age = 36 and double price = 9.5, then print Age 36 price 9.50.
walkthrough:
int age = 36; makes a whole-number variable. double price = 9.5; makes a floating-point one. The type goes before the name.
In the printf format string, %d is a slot for an int and %.2f is a slot for a double shown with 2 digits after the point.
The values after the string fill the slots in order: age goes into %d, price into %.2f.
9.5 with two decimals is 9.50, so the line reads Age 36 price 9.50.
Common mistake: using %d for the double. The type does not match the slot, which is undefined behaviour, and you usually see a nonsense number.

title: Count to five
task: Use a for loop to print 1 to 5, one per line.
walkthrough:
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) has three parts split by ;. Start: i is 1. Test: keep going while i <= 5. Step: i++ adds 1 after each run.
The block in { } runs once for each value of i.
printf("%d\n", i) prints the current i and a newline, so you get 1 to 5 on separate lines.
When i becomes 6 the test fails and the loop ends.
Common mistake: writing i < 5. Then 5 fails the test and the output stops at 4.

title: Sum an array
task: Add up the array {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42} and print the total.
walkthrough:
int nums[] = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42}; makes an array of ints. The empty [] lets the compiler count the size, here 6.
int total = 0; starts the sum at zero.
The for loop goes i = 0 to 5. Array positions start at 0, so nums[0] is 4 and nums[5] is 42.
total += nums[i] adds each item to total. Without { }, the loop body is just that one statement.
4 + 8 + 15 + 16 + 23 + 42 = 108, which printf prints.
Common mistake: writing i <= 6. nums[6] is past the end of the array, which is undefined behaviour, and C will not stop you.

title: A function
task: Write int max(int a, int b) and print max(3, 9).
walkthrough:
int max(int a, int b) is a function that takes two ints and returns an int.
a > b ? a : b is the conditional operator: if a > b is true the result is a, otherwise it is b.
return sends that bigger value back.
In main, max(3, 9) compares 3 > 9, which is false, so it gives 9, and printf prints 9.
Common mistake: putting max below main with no declaration above it. Modern C does not allow calling an undeclared function, so the compiler warns or errors.

title: Swap with pointers
task: Write void swap(int *a, int *b). Swap x = 1 and y = 2, then print x=2 y=1.
walkthrough:
void swap(int *a, int *b) takes two pointers. void means it returns nothing.
int t = *a; follows a and saves the value it points at. *a = *b; copies the second value over the first. *b = t; puts the saved value in the second.
In main, swap(&x, &y) passes the addresses of x and y, so the function works on the real x and y, not copies.
After the call x is 2 and y is 1, and printf prints x=2 y=1.
Common mistake: writing swap with plain int a, int b. C passes copies, so only the copies are swapped and main still prints x=1 y=2.

title: A struct
task: Make a struct with name and age for Ada, 36. Print Ada is 36.
walkthrough:
struct { ... } groups several values into one: here a name, which is an array of 20 chars, and an int age.
typedef gives that struct the short name Person, so you can write Person instead of the full struct type.
Person p = {"Ada", 36}; fills the fields in order: name gets "Ada", age gets 36.
p.name and p.age read the fields with a dot. %s prints a string, %d an int, giving Ada is 36.
Common mistake: forgetting the ; after } Person. The compiler errors, usually pointing at the line after it.

title: Reverse a string
task: Reverse the text "hello" in place and print olleh.
walkthrough:
char s[] = "hello"; makes a char array holding h e l l o plus a hidden '\0' that marks the end of the string.
strlen(s), from <string.h>, counts the characters before the '\0', so n is 5.
The loop runs while i < n / 2. With ints, 5 / 2 is 2, so it runs for i = 0 and 1; the middle l stays put.
Each pass swaps s[i] with s[n - 1 - i] through a temporary t: first h and o, then e and the second l.
printf with %s prints the changed array: olleh.
Common mistake: looping to i < n instead of n / 2. Every pair gets swapped twice, so the string ends up back as hello.

title: Core: a reference
task: Write void twice(int &n) that doubles n. Call it on x = 4 and print x with std::cout.
remember: & in a type = the same one.
walkthrough:
void twice(int &n) takes a reference. The & here means n is another name for the caller's variable, not a copy.
n = n * 2; therefore changes the caller's variable directly.
In main, x is 4. twice(x) passes x by reference, so after the call x is 8.
std::cout << x << "\n" sends x and then a newline to the output stream. std:: says cout lives in the standard namespace.
Common mistake: dropping the & and writing int n. Then twice doubles a copy, and the program prints 4.

title: Core: a template
task: Write template <typename T> T first(T a, T b) that returns a. Print first(1, 2) and first('a', 'b') on one line with a space between.
remember: <T> = any type goes here.
walkthrough:
template <typename T> says the function below works for some type T that is filled in later.
T first(T a, T b) takes two values of type T and returns one of type T. Here it just returns a.
first(1, 2): both are ints, so the compiler makes an int version and it returns 1.
first('a', 'b'): both are chars, so it makes a char version that returns 'a', and cout prints a char as its letter.
The << pieces print 1, a space, then a, giving 1 a.
Common mistake: calling first(1, 'b'). The compiler sees int for one T and char for the other, cannot pick one, and gives a no matching function error.

title: Say hello
task: Print Hello, world! with std::cout.
walkthrough:
#include <iostream> brings in C++ input and output streams.
int main() is where the program starts. Its body is inside { }.
std::cout is the standard output stream. std:: means it is in the standard namespace. << sends the text into it.
\n at the end of the string starts a new line. return 0; reports success.
Common mistake: writing cout without std:: and without a using line. The compiler says cout is not declared.

title: Strings
task: Make std::string name = "Ada" and print Hi Ada.
walkthrough:
#include <string> brings in std::string, a string type that manages its own memory.
std::string name = "Ada"; makes a string object named name, built from the text Ada.
std::cout << "Hi " << name << "\n" chains three pieces into the output: the text Hi with its space, then the name, then a newline.
The output is Hi Ada.
Common mistake: leaving out #include <string>. It may compile by luck because another header pulls it in, but that is not guaranteed, so always include what you use.

title: Vector loop
task: Make a vector {1, 2, 3} and print each number with a range-for, one per line.
walkthrough:
std::vector<int> is a growable array of ints. The <int> is a template argument saying what it holds.
= {1, 2, 3} fills it with three values.
for (int n : nums) is a range-based for loop: it puts each element in n, in order.
The body has no { } because it is one statement: print n and a newline. So you get 1, 2 and 3 on separate lines.
Common mistake: writing for (int n in nums) out of Python habit. C++ uses a colon there, and in is a compile error.

title: Sort
task: Sort the vector {5, 2, 9, 1} and print it on one line separated by spaces.
walkthrough:
std::vector<int> v = {5, 2, 9, 1}; makes a vector with four ints.
std::sort, from <algorithm>, sorts a range. v.begin() points at the first element and v.end() points just past the last.
By default it puts the values in ascending order, so v becomes 1, 2, 5, 9.
The loop prints each value followed by a space, then a final "\n" ends the line.
Common mistake: calling std::sort(v). In C++17 std::sort needs the two iterators, so passing the vector alone does not compile.

title: A class
task: Make a class Rectangle with width and height and an area() method. Print the area of 3 x 4.
walkthrough:
class Rectangle { ... }; defines a new type. public: parts can be used from outside; private: parts only from inside the class.
Rectangle(int w, int h) : w(w), h(h) {} is the constructor. After the colon, each member is set from the parameter with the same name.
int area() const returns w * h. const promises this method does not change the object.
Rectangle r(3, 4); calls the constructor, so w is 3 and h is 4. r.area() gives 12, which cout prints.
Common mistake: forgetting the ; after the closing } of the class. The compiler errors, often with a confusing message on the next line.

title: Word count with map
task: Count the words in "the cat and the hat" with std::map and print each word and count, one per line (map sorts them).
walkthrough:
std::map<std::string, int> maps each word to a count. A map keeps its keys sorted.
std::stringstream ss(...) treats the string like an input stream. ss >> word reads one space-separated word at a time.
while (ss >> word) keeps going until no words are left. counts[word]++ adds a new key with value 0 if missing, then adds 1.
for (const auto& [w, n] : counts) walks the map in key order and splits each pair into w and n. That [ ] form is a structured binding, from C++17.
Sorted alphabetically, the output is and 1, cat 1, hat 1, the 2.
Common mistake: expecting the words in the order they appeared. std::map always sorts by key, so and comes first.

title: Shapes
task: Make an abstract Shape with virtual area(), and Square and Circle (use 3.14). Print the areas of Square(2) and Circle(1).
walkthrough:
Shape has virtual double area() const = 0; which is a pure virtual method. Shape is now abstract: you cannot make a plain Shape.
virtual ~Shape() = default; makes the destructor virtual, so deleting a Square or Circle through a Shape pointer cleans up correctly.
Square and Circle inherit from Shape with : public Shape and each writes its own area. override asks the compiler to check that it really replaces the base method.
The vector holds std::unique_ptr<Shape>, smart pointers that delete their object automatically. std::make_unique<Square>(2) builds a Square with side 2.
s->area() calls the right version at run time: 2 * 2 = 4 and 3.14 * 1 * 1 = 3.14. cout prints the double 4.0 as 4.
Common mistake: leaving off const on Square's area. It no longer matches the base method, so override makes it a compile error.

title: A template
task: Write a template function biggest(a, b). Print biggest(3, 7) and biggest(2.5, 1.5).
walkthrough:
template <typename T> makes biggest work for any type T that supports >.
a > b ? a : b returns a if it is bigger, otherwise b.
biggest(3, 7): both ints, so T is int and it returns 7.
biggest(2.5, 1.5): both doubles, so T is double and it returns 2.5.
cout prints 7, a space, then 2.5, giving 7 2.5.
Common mistake: calling biggest("apple", "pear"). T becomes const char*, so > compares memory addresses, not letters, and the answer means nothing.

title: Core: command, flags, argument
task: List everything (all files, long format) in the Desktop folder, using joined flags.
solution: ls -la Desktop
remember: What, how, on what.
walkthrough:
ls is the command: it lists what is inside a folder.
-la is two flags joined: -l means long format (one line per item, with size, owner and date), -a means all, so hidden files that start with a dot show too. It is the same as typing -l -a.
Desktop is the argument: the folder to look in. It is a relative path, so it works when you are in your home folder (~).
You see a line for every item, including . (this folder) and .. (the folder above).
Common mistake: leaving out the space, as in ls-la Desktop. The shell looks for a command called ls-la and says command not found.

title: Core: a pipe
task: Print the file notes.txt and pipe it into wc -l to count its lines.
solution: cat notes.txt | wc -l
remember: | passes it to the next.
walkthrough:
cat notes.txt prints the file's text. Normally that text goes to your screen.
The pipe | takes that output and feeds it into the next command instead of the screen.
wc is word count, and the -l flag tells it to count only lines. It reads the text coming through the pipe, so it needs no file name.
You see one number: how many lines notes.txt has.
Common mistake: trusting the number when the last line has no newline at the end. wc -l counts newline characters, so it comes out one short.

title: Where am I?
task: Show the folder you are in, then list the files in it.
solution:
pwd
ls
walkthrough:
pwd means print working directory. It shows the full path of the folder you are in, like /Users/you.
That folder is what . means in a path, and every relative path starts from it.
ls with no argument lists the folder you are in right now.
Run these two whenever you feel lost: first where am I, then what is here.
Common mistake: expecting ls to show everything. Hidden files like .git or .zshrc only show with ls -a.

title: Go to the Desktop
task: Move into the Desktop folder, then list what's there.
solution:
cd Desktop
ls
walkthrough:
cd means change directory. Desktop is the argument: the folder to move into.
Desktop is a relative path, so the shell looks for it inside the folder you are in. From your home folder (~) that works.
cd prints nothing when it succeeds. The prompt changes to show the new folder.
ls then lists what is on your Desktop. To go back up one level, cd .. moves to the parent folder.
Common mistake: running cd Desktop from some other folder. zsh says no such file or directory, because there is no Desktop there. cd ~/Desktop works from anywhere.

title: A new project
task: Make a folder called my-site, go into it, and make an empty index.html.
solution:
mkdir my-site
cd my-site
touch index.html
walkthrough:
mkdir means make directory. my-site is the name of the new folder, made inside the folder you are in.
cd my-site moves you into it, so the next command happens there.
touch index.html creates an empty file with that name. If the file already exists, touch leaves its contents alone and only updates its date.
None of the three prints anything when it works. Run ls to see the file.
Common mistake: a name with a space, like mkdir my site. The space splits it into two arguments, so you get two folders, my and site. Use a dash or put the name in quotes.

title: Write into a file
task: Write the line hello into notes.txt with echo, then show the file.
solution:
echo hello > notes.txt
cat notes.txt
walkthrough:
echo prints its argument, here the word hello.
> is a redirect: instead of the screen, the output goes into the file notes.txt. If the file does not exist, it is created.
cat notes.txt prints the file, so you see hello and can check it worked.
Common mistake: using > when you meant to add a line. > replaces everything already in the file. >> adds to the end instead.

title: Copy and rename
task: Copy notes.txt to backup.txt, then rename backup.txt to old.txt.
solution:
cp notes.txt backup.txt
mv backup.txt old.txt
walkthrough:
cp means copy. It takes two arguments: the source first, then the destination. Now notes.txt and backup.txt are two separate files with the same text.
mv means move. When the destination is a new name in the same folder, moving is renaming. backup.txt is gone and old.txt has its contents.
Both commands print nothing when they work. Run ls to see the result.
Common mistake: copying or moving onto a name that already exists. cp and mv replace that file without asking. Add -i if you want them to ask first.

title: Search
task: Search every file in this folder and below for TODO, showing line numbers.
solution: grep -rn TODO .
walkthrough:
grep searches text for a pattern and prints the lines that match.
-rn is two flags joined: -r means recursive (go into every folder below), -n means show the line number of each match.
TODO is the pattern, and . is the argument: start searching here, in the current folder.
Each result looks like path:line number:the matching line.
Common mistake: expecting it to also find todo or Todo. grep is case-sensitive. Add -i to ignore case.

title: Clean up
task: Make a folder trash-me with a file inside, then delete the whole folder.
solution:
mkdir trash-me
touch trash-me/file.txt
rm -r trash-me
walkthrough:
mkdir trash-me makes the folder.
touch trash-me/file.txt makes an empty file inside it. The / in the path means inside.
rm means remove. -r means recursive: delete the folder and everything inside it.
rm does not use the Trash. What it deletes is gone, so read the path twice before you press Return.
Common mistake: rm trash-me without -r. rm refuses and says trash-me is a directory.

title: Save with git
task: Check what changed, add everything, commit with the message "First commit", and push.
solution:
git status
git add .
git commit -m "First commit"
git push
walkthrough:
git status shows what changed in your working folder and what is already staged. It changes nothing.
git add . puts every change in this folder and below into the staging area. The . means here.
git commit -m "First commit" saves the staged changes as one snapshot in your history, with that message. The quotes keep the two words as one argument.
git push sends your new commits to the remote, usually called origin, for example GitHub.
Common mistake: git push before git commit. Git says Everything up-to-date, because push only sends commits, and there is no new one.

title: Core: brew + subcommand
task: Show information about the git formula, then install the app firefox as a cask.
solution:
brew info git
brew install --cask firefox
remember: brew + what to do + to what.
walkthrough:
Every Homebrew command has the same shape: brew, then a subcommand that says what to do, then the package name.
brew info git shows details about the git formula: its version, what it depends on, and whether it is installed.
A formula is a command-line tool you run in the terminal. A cask is a regular Mac app with a window, which goes into /Applications.
brew install --cask firefox installs Firefox as a cask. --cask is the flag that says I mean the app.
Common mistake: putting the words in the wrong order, like brew git info. Homebrew reads git as the subcommand and says unknown command.

title: What do I have?
task: List everything Homebrew has installed.
solution: brew list
walkthrough:
brew is the command, list is the subcommand.
It shows what Homebrew itself has installed, with formulae (command-line tools) and casks (apps) in separate groups.
It takes no argument here because you are asking about everything.
Common mistake: expecting to see every app on your Mac. Apps you installed from the App Store or a download do not appear, because Homebrew did not install them.

title: Install a tool
task: Install the package tree.
solution: brew install tree
walkthrough:
brew is the command, install is the subcommand, and tree is the argument: the formula to install.
tree is a command-line tool, so it is a formula and needs no --cask.
Homebrew downloads it, plus anything it depends on, and puts the command on your path.
After it finishes, typing tree prints the folders and files below you as a tree.
Common mistake: typing sudo brew install. Homebrew refuses to run as root. Run brew as your normal user.

title: Install an app
task: Install the app visual-studio-code (it is a cask).
solution: brew install --cask visual-studio-code
walkthrough:
brew install is the usual install command. visual-studio-code is the argument: the name of the cask.
--cask is the flag that says this is an app, not a command-line tool. Homebrew puts it in /Applications like a normal app.
If a formula and a cask have the same name, brew install picks the formula. --cask makes sure you get the app.
Common mistake: guessing the name, like vscode. Homebrew says it cannot find it. Run brew search code first to see the exact name.

title: Learn about a package
task: Search for python, then show the info for python.
solution:
brew search python
brew info python
walkthrough:
brew search python looks through package names and prints the formulae and casks that contain python.
Use it when you do not know the exact name. It installs nothing.
brew info python then shows details for that one package: the version, a short description, what it depends on, and whether you have it installed.
Search first to find the name, info next to check it, install last.
Common mistake: expecting search to match what a package does. It matches names. Add --desc to search the descriptions too.

title: Update everything
task: Update Homebrew itself, then upgrade all your packages.
solution:
brew update
brew upgrade
walkthrough:
brew update downloads the newest version of Homebrew and its list of packages. It does not change your installed tools.
brew upgrade then installs newer versions of every package you have that is out of date.
With no argument, upgrade does all of them. brew upgrade tree would do only tree.
Common mistake: thinking brew update upgraded your tools. It only refreshed the list. You need brew upgrade for that.

title: Remove a package
task: Uninstall tree, then clean up old downloads.
solution:
brew uninstall tree
brew cleanup
walkthrough:
brew uninstall tree removes the tree formula. The tree command stops working.
brew cleanup deletes old versions of your packages and old downloads Homebrew kept in its cache. It frees disk space.
Neither needs --cask here, because tree is a formula.
Common mistake: uninstalling a package that another one you have depends on. Homebrew refuses and tells you which package still needs it.

title: Health check
task: Check your Homebrew for problems.
solution: brew doctor
walkthrough:
brew is the command, doctor is the subcommand. It checks your Homebrew setup for known problems.
It changes nothing. It only prints warnings, each with a hint on how to fix it.
If all is well, it says Your system is ready to brew.
Run it when an install fails in a way you do not understand.
Common mistake: panicking over every warning. Homebrew itself says that if everything you use works fine, you can leave a warning alone.

title: Background service
task: Start the postgresql service, then stop it.
solution:
brew services start postgresql
brew services stop postgresql
walkthrough:
Some formulae are servers that run in the background, like the postgresql database.
brew services is the subcommand for them. start is the action, postgresql the argument.
start runs it now and also each time you log in.
stop shuts it down and stops it from starting at login.
brew services list shows what is running.
Common mistake: forgetting to stop it. The database keeps running in the background and starts again every time you log in.

title: Core: the three places
task: Stage the file index.html, then commit it with the message "first".
solution:
git add index.html
git commit -m "first"
remember: add packs the box, commit seals it.
walkthrough:
git add index.html puts that file in the staging area: the box of changes for your next commit.
git commit saves everything in the staging area as one snapshot in the history.
-m is a flag meaning message, and "first" is the message. The quotes keep it as one argument.
Common mistake: committing without git add first. Git then says nothing to commit, because the staging area is empty.

title: Core: a remote
task: Send your main branch to origin.
solution: git push origin main
remember: push up, origin = GitHub.
walkthrough:
git push sends commits from your history to a remote, a copy of the project on another computer such as GitHub.
origin is the first argument: the name of the remote. origin is just the usual name for the place you cloned from or connected to.
main is the second argument: the branch to send.
Git prints the commits it sent, or Everything up-to-date if there was nothing new.
Common mistake: pushing main when your branch is called master. Git says src refspec main does not match any, because you have no branch named main. git branch shows your branch names.

title: Who are you?
task: Tell Git your name and your email (do this once per computer).
solution:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
walkthrough:
git config is the subcommand for Git's settings. --global means save it for your user on this computer, in the file ~/.gitconfig, so every project uses it.
user.name is the setting, and "Your Name" is the value. The quotes keep the two words together as one argument.
The second line does the same for user.email.
Git writes this name and email into every commit you make. Both commands print nothing when they work.
Common mistake: leaving out --global. Then the setting is saved only for the project you are in, and outside a project Git refuses.

title: Start a project
task: Turn this folder into a Git project, then check its status.
solution:
git init
git status
walkthrough:
git init turns the folder you are in into a Git project. It creates a hidden folder called .git, where the history will live.
Your files are not saved yet. They sit in the working folder, and Git just knows about the folder now.
git status shows the branch you are on, says No commits yet, and lists your files as untracked: Git sees them but is not saving them.
Common mistake: running git init in your home folder by accident. Then everything in your home is one big project. Check with pwd first.

title: Your first commit
task: Add index.html, then commit it with the message "Add home page".
solution:
git add index.html
git commit -m "Add home page"
walkthrough:
git add index.html moves the file from your working folder into the staging area.
