git commit takes what is staged and saves it as one snapshot in the history.
-m "Add home page" gives the snapshot its message. The quotes keep the three words as one argument.
Git prints the branch, a short commit id and how many files changed.
Common mistake: git commit without -m. Git opens a text editor, often Vim, to ask for the message. To get out of Vim without saving, press Esc, type :q! and press Return.

title: Look back
task: Show the lines you changed but have not added yet, then show the history, one commit per line.
solution:
git diff
git log --oneline
walkthrough:
git diff shows changes in your working folder that are not staged yet. Lines starting with - were removed, lines with + were added.
git log shows the history, newest commit first.
--oneline is a flag that squeezes each commit onto one line: a short id and the first line of the message.
If the output is long, Git shows it a page at a time. Press q to get back to the prompt.
Common mistake: running git diff after git add and seeing nothing. The change is staged now, so plain diff skips it. git diff --staged shows it.

title: Connect to GitHub
task: Connect this project to https://github.com/you/my-site.git as origin, then push main for the first time.
solution:
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/my-site.git
git push -u origin main
walkthrough:
git remote add saves a remote: a name and the address it stands for. origin is the name, the URL is the address.
Nothing is sent yet. Git just remembers where origin is.
git push -u origin main sends your main branch to origin.
-u links your main to origin's main. After that, plain git push and git pull know where to go.
Common mistake: running git remote add origin a second time. Git says remote origin already exists. To change the address, use git remote set-url origin with the new URL.

title: Oops, un-add it
task: You ran git add on secret.txt by mistake. Take it out of the next commit, but keep the file as it is.
solution: git restore --staged secret.txt
walkthrough:
git restore puts files back. --staged is the flag that says work on the staging area.
secret.txt is the argument: the file to take out of the staging area.
The file stays in your working folder exactly as it is. It just will not be in the next commit.
git status now lists it as not staged, or untracked if it is a new file.
Common mistake: leaving out --staged. Then git restore works on your working folder instead and throws away edits in the file that were not staged.

title: Try an idea on a branch
task: Make a branch called new-header and move to it. Add everything and commit "Change header". Go back to main and merge new-header into it.
solution:
git switch -c new-header
git add .
git commit -m "Change header"
git switch main
git merge new-header
walkthrough:
git switch -c new-header creates a branch called new-header and moves you onto it. -c means create.
git add . stages everything, and git commit -m "Change header" saves it on new-header only. main does not have it yet.
git switch main moves you back. Your files change back to how main has them.
git merge new-header brings the commits from new-header into the branch you are on, which is main.
Common mistake: running git merge while still on new-header. That merges main into new-header, main stays as it was, and Git says Already up to date.

title: Undo a pushed commit
task: Commit 1a2b3c4 broke the site and it is already on GitHub. Undo it the safe way, then send the fix to GitHub.
solution:
git revert 1a2b3c4
git push
walkthrough:
git revert 1a2b3c4 makes a new commit that undoes the changes of commit 1a2b3c4. The old commit stays in the history.
1a2b3c4 is the argument: the short id of the bad commit, which you can find with git log --oneline.
Git opens an editor with a ready-made message. Save and close it to finish.
git push sends the new undo commit to GitHub. Nothing that is already there gets rewritten, so it is safe for everyone.
Common mistake: using git reset to remove a commit that is already pushed. Your next git push is rejected, because your history no longer matches GitHub's.
